name: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
title: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
answer: Agent negotiation in over-the-counter markets covers software agents that quote, counterquote, and agree terms for instruments traded bilaterally rather than on a central limit order book. It spans dealer-to-client request-for-quote, interdealer brokerage, and voice or chat workflows that are increasingly transcribed and parsed into structured messages. Typical instruments include corporate and government bonds, interest rate and credit swaps, repos, foreign exchange forwards, and structured notes. The scope also includes pre-trade credit checks, inventory and risk limits, and post-trade affirmation, because negotiation in OTC markets is inseparable from the surrounding workflow.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Agent negotiation in over-the-counter markets covers software agents that quote, counterquote, and agree terms for instruments traded bilaterally rather than on a central limit order book. It spans dealer-to-client request-for-quote, interdealer brokerage, and voice or chat workflows that are increasingly transcribed and parsed into structured messages. Typical instruments include corporate and government bonds, interest rate and credit swaps, repos, foreign exchange forwards, and structured notes. The scope also includes pre-trade credit checks, inventory and risk limits, and post-trade affirmation, because negotiation in OTC markets is inseparable from the surrounding workflow.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Agents run on electronic trading venues, dealer platforms, and internal orchestration layers that connect to market data, pricing engines, counterparty credit systems, and order management systems. Common inputs include real-time quotes, reference data, historical trades, and client axes, often delivered through APIs, FIX, or chat protocols. The agent itself may be a rules-based bot, a large language model with tool access, or a hybrid that uses deterministic pricing and a language layer for dialogue. Compute may be cloud or on-premises, with low-latency paths for pricing and separate paths for natural language processing. Audit logs, message buses, and identity services are part of the runtime, not add-ons.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a request, a dealer quote, or an indicative price, then the agent parses the message, checks credit and limits, and proposes a price or terms. Negotiation can be single-issue, such as price, or multi-issue, such as size, settlement date, collateral, and fees. Agents may use game-theoretic strategies, reinforcement learning, or scripted playbooks, and they often need to explain a quote or a rejection to a human supervisor. Human traders remain in the loop for exceptions, large tickets, and relationship-sensitive clients. The outcome is a confirmed trade or a clear pass, with the rationale recorded for later review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in agent negotiation turn on authority, consent, and recordkeeping. Firms need to define what an agent may commit, how counterparties are identified, and what disclosures apply when a machine negotiates on behalf of a dealer or client. Provenance matters because regulators and internal reviewers may ask which model, data, and instructions produced a quote, and whether the agent followed venue rules and market conduct standards. Risks include unintended collusion, price signaling, data leakage, model error, and unclear liability when a trade is disputed. Controls typically include pre-trade limits, kill switches, human approval thresholds, and immutable logs.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Adoption is likely to grow first in liquid, standardized OTC products where messages are already electronic, then in less liquid segments where chat and voice still dominate. Expect more agent-to-agent negotiation, but also more emphasis on interoperability, standard message schemas, and auditability across venues. Model improvements may shift agents from quoting assistance to fuller negotiation, while regulation and market structure will shape how much autonomy is permitted. The practical direction is not full automation of every OTC trade, but a tighter loop among pricing, credit, negotiation, and post-trade processing.
